prompt: `readConfig` returns `fmt.Errorf("read config: %w", err)`. What is that return value?
hint: Section 02's loop printed it, and then printed what was inside it.

choices.text: A longer string with both messages joined
choices.why: The message is longer, but the value is an error, a `*fmt.wrapError`, and the loop found `err` inside it.

choices.text: A new error that holds `err` and adds words
choices.why: Right. `errors.Unwrap` on it gave back the `*fs.PathError` that `os.ReadFile` returned, whole.

choices.text: `err` itself, with its message changed in place to start with `read config`
choices.why: Nothing changed `err`: the loop printed the `*fs.PathError` with its own message, `open settings.json: ...`, untouched.

choices.text: A copy of `err`, of the same type, with a new message
choices.why: The type changed: the loop printed `*fmt.wrapError` for it, and `*fs.PathError` one line further down.

prompt: When does `errors.Unwrap(e)` return `nil`?
hint: It calls one method, if it can.

choices.text: When `e` is the outermost error of a chain
choices.why: The outermost link is the one with the most inside it; the loop unwrapped it first.

choices.text: When `e` was made with `%w`
choices.why: That is exactly the case where it returns something: `%w` gives the error an `Unwrap` method.

choices.text: When `e` has no method `Unwrap() error`
choices.why: Right. `syscall.Errno` has no such method, which is why the loop stopped after it.

choices.text: When the message of `e` is empty
choices.why: `errors.Unwrap` never reads the message; it looks for a method.

prompt: Put the links of the error `start` returned in the order section 02's loop printed them.
hint: The loop begins with what `main` received.

prompt: `both := errors.Join(fs.ErrNotExist, fs.ErrPermission)`. What does `errors.Unwrap(both)` return?
hint: A joined error has an `Unwrap` method, but which one?

choices.text: `fs.ErrNotExist`, the first error given to `Join`
choices.why: That assumes it unwraps one link at a time from a list; it does not touch a list at all.

choices.text: `nil`
choices.why: Right. The joined error's method is `Unwrap() []error`, and `errors.Unwrap` only calls `Unwrap() error`.

choices.text: A slice with both errors
choices.why: The joined error's own method returns that slice, but `errors.Unwrap` returns an `error`, and gave `<nil>`.

choices.text: `fs.ErrPermission`, the last error given to `Join`
choices.why: The order is not the problem: `errors.Unwrap` does not open a list of errors at either end.

prompt: A program wraps the error from `os.ReadFile` of a missing file with `%w` three times, in three functions, instead of twice. How many lines does section 02's loop print, not counting the `fmt.Println(err)` line before it?
hint: Count the wrappers, then what `os.ReadFile` itself returned.

prompt: In section 03, `err == fs.ErrNotExist` printed `false` although the file was missing. Why?
hint: What is the value `start` returned?

choices.text: `==` compares the two messages, and they differ
choices.why: `==` compares the values, not their text; and two different values with the same text would still be unequal.

choices.text: `err` is the outermost wrapper, a different value
choices.why: Right. `==` looks at that one value, and it is a `*fmt.wrapError`, whatever it holds.

choices.text: Errors cannot be compared with `==`; it only works for `nil`
choices.why: The comparison compiled and ran, and section 03 also compared an `Errno` with `==` and got `true`.

choices.text: `fs.ErrNotExist` belongs to `io/fs`, and `os` has its own
choices.why: `os.ErrNotExist` is `fs.ErrNotExist` under another name, as `go doc` showed.

prompt: `errors.___(err, fs.ErrNotExist)` walks every link of the chain looking for the missing-file error.
hint: It answers true or false.

prompt: For the chain of a missing `settings.json`, what does `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrPermission)` return?
hint: Is a missing file a permission problem?

choices.text: `true`, because the chain holds an error
choices.why: `errors.Is` does not ask whether there is an error, but whether this particular one is in there.

choices.text: `true`, because every file-system error matches every `fs` variable
choices.why: `syscall.ENOENT`'s `Is` method says yes to `fs.ErrNotExist` only; it is answered per target.

choices.text: `false`
choices.why: Right. Section 03 printed `permission    false`: no link is, or claims to be, a permission error.

choices.text: It panics, since the target is not in the chain
choices.why: A target that is not there is the ordinary `false` case; nothing panics.

prompt: The chain's last link is `syscall.ENOENT`, which is not equal to `fs.ErrNotExist`. Why does `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)` still say `true`?
hint: Equality is one of two ways a link can match.

choices.text: `errors.Is` compares the messages, and both say the file is missing
choices.why: The messages differ, `file does not exist` against `no such file or directory`, and `Is` does not read them.

choices.text: `syscall.Errno` has an `Is` method that says yes to it
choices.why: Right. A link matches if it equals the target or its own `Is` method claims it; `ENOENT.Is(fs.ErrNotExist)` printed `true`.

choices.text: `fs.ErrNotExist` and `syscall.ENOENT` are one variable
choices.why: That is true of `os.ErrNotExist`; `inner == fs.ErrNotExist` printed `false` for `ENOENT`.

choices.text: `errors.Is` skips the last link and only checks wrappers
choices.why: It checks every link, the last one included; that last one is where the match came from.

prompt: A colleague changes `%w` to `%v` in `readConfig` to "tidy the message". The program prints exactly the same text. What breaks?
hint: Who looks at an error other than a person?

choices.text: Nothing: the message is identical, so the error is too
choices.why: Section 03 printed the same first line and a two-link chain; equal text is not an equal chain.

choices.text: The build: `%v` cannot format an error value
choices.why: `%v` formats any value, an error included; the program compiled and ran.

choices.text: `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)` turns false, so the defaults branch never runs
choices.why: Right. The `*fs.PathError` and the `Errno` are gone from the chain, and the code that inspected it takes the other branch.

choices.text: Only the type printed by `%T`, which no code reads
choices.why: The type changed to `*errors.errorString`, and every function that walks the chain reads exactly that.

prompt: Why does section 04 write `errors.As(err, &pe)` rather than `errors.As(err, pe)`?
hint: What does `As` do with what it finds?

choices.text: `As` writes the link it finds into the variable
choices.why: Right. Without the `&` it had nowhere to write, and the program panicked.

choices.text: The `&` makes the call faster by not copying `pe`
choices.why: `pe` is one pointer; copying it costs nothing. The `&` is about where the result goes.

choices.text: The `&` tells `As` to look deeper than one link
choices.why: `As` always walks the whole chain; the `&` changes nothing about the search.

choices.text: Both work; `&pe` is the usual style
choices.why: Without it, `go vet` reported the call and the program panicked: `target must be a non-nil pointer`.

prompt: `errors.AsType[fs.PathError](err)` does not compile. What does the error message blame?
hint: Which type has the `Error` method?

choices.text: `AsType` accepts only interface types between its brackets, never a struct type
choices.why: `*fs.PathError` is a pointer to a struct and works; the constraint is `error`, not "an interface".

choices.text: `fs.PathError` is unexported
choices.why: Its capital P exports it, and `go doc` printed its fields.

choices.text: `Error` has a pointer receiver, so only the pointer is an `error`
choices.why: Right. Only `*fs.PathError` satisfies `error`, which is lesson 26's method-set rule.

choices.text: A type from another package cannot be a type argument
choices.why: `*fs.PathError`, from the same package, worked in the same position one program earlier.

prompt: Match each function to what it gives back.
hint: Two of them answer the same question in different shapes.

pairs.right: a `bool`: is this value in the chain
a `bool`, and `v` filled with the first link of its type
the first link of type `T`, and a `bool`

right_distractors: the message with the context removed

prompt: A command must tell the user which file it could not open, and the error it holds reads `start server: read config: open settings.json: no such file or directory`. Which way of getting `settings.json` keeps working when somebody adds another layer of context?
hint: The path is a field somewhere in the chain.

choices.text: Split the message on `": "` and take the third piece
choices.why: A new layer adds one more piece in front, and the third piece becomes `read config`.

choices.text: `err.(*fs.PathError)`, then its `Path`
choices.why: The assertion sees only the outside value; section 04 printed `assertion: false` before any layer was added.

choices.text: `errors.AsType[*fs.PathError](err)`, then `.Path` of the result
choices.why: Right. It walks the chain to the `*fs.PathError` however deep it sits, and reads a field rather than text.

choices.text: `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)`, then the word after `open`
choices.why: `Is` only says the file is missing; the name still comes from parsing a message that may change.

prompt: `var pe *fs.PathError` and then `errors.As(err, pe)`, with no `&`. Which of these are true? Select all that apply.
hint: Three tools looked at it in section 04.

choices.text: It compiles
choices.why: Yes. The target parameter is `any`, so the compiler accepts any value there.

choices.text: `go vet` always reports the call
choices.why: Yes: `second argument to errors.As must be a non-nil pointer ...`, with exit status 1.

choices.text: It returns `false` quietly and the program goes on
choices.why: It panics with `errors: target must be a non-nil pointer`, and the program stops with status 2.

choices.text: The compiler refuses it with a type error
choices.why: That is what `AsType` buys you; `As` takes `any`, and `any` accepts it.

prompt: A library you call now returns `fmt.Errorf("load %s: %w", name, err)` around an `os.Open` error. Your old code checks `os.IsNotExist(err)` and has stopped noticing missing files. What is the fix?
hint: Read what `go doc os.IsNotExist` says new code should use.

choices.text: Ask the library to wrap with `%v` instead
choices.why: With `%v` there is no chain at all, and `os.IsNotExist` still sees a `*errors.errorString`.

choices.text: Replace it with `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)`
choices.why: Right. `errors.Is` walks the chain; `os.IsNotExist` predates wrapping and looks at the outside only.

choices.text: Compare `err == os.ErrNotExist`
choices.why: `==` sees the outermost wrapper, exactly like `os.IsNotExist`, and is false for the same reason.

choices.text: Compare `errors.Unwrap(err) == fs.ErrNotExist`
choices.why: One unwrap reaches the `*fs.PathError`, which is not `fs.ErrNotExist`; it matches only through `Is` further down.

prompt: `err` came from `os.ReadFile` on a missing file. Which of these return an error in which `errors.Is(..., fs.ErrNotExist)` still finds it? Select all that apply.
hint: Which of them keep `err` itself, and which keep only its text?

choices.text: `fmt.Errorf("load: %w", err)`
choices.why: Yes. `%w` keeps `err` as the next link.

choices.text: `errors.Join(err, cleanupErr)`
choices.why: Yes. A joined error is a tree, and `errors.Is` walks every branch of it.

choices.text: `fmt.Errorf("load: %v", err)`
choices.why: `%v` copies the text into a `*errors.errorString` and drops `err`, as section 03's cut chain showed.

choices.text: `errors.New("load: " + err.Error())`
choices.why: Same as `%v`: a new error holding a string, with nothing to unwrap.

prompt: Any error type becomes a wrapper by having a method `___() error` that returns the error it holds.
hint: Section 02's `*fmt.wrapError` and `*fs.PathError` both have it.

prompt: Your package has `type QuotaError struct{ User string }` with `Error` on `*QuotaError`, and callers wrap it twice with `%w`. How does the top of the program read `User`?
hint: It is the same question as the path in `*fs.PathError`.

choices.text: `errors.Is(err, &QuotaError{})`, and then read the `User` field of the error
choices.why: `Is` compares values, and a freshly made pointer equals no link; even a `true` would hand you no field.

choices.text: `errors.Unwrap(err).(*QuotaError)`
choices.why: One unwrap removes one layer of two, so the assertion meets the second wrapper.

choices.text: `errors.AsType[*QuotaError](err)` and the `User` of the result
choices.why: Right. It finds the link by type at any depth, exactly as with `*fs.PathError`.

choices.text: `err.(*QuotaError)` straight away
choices.why: The outside value is a `*fmt.wrapError`, and the assertion looks at nothing else.

prompt: With `%v` in `readConfig` and `%w` in `start`, how many links did section 03's loop print?
hint: Count the lines with a type in front.
